KEY MESSAGE 1...Mostly cloudy with periods of off-and-on light 
showers tonight into early Sunday, before trending mostly sunny by 
Sunday afternoon. High risk for rip currents along the eastern 
coast, with minor coastal flooding around the evening high tide 
tonight and Sunday night for the Cape and Islands.

Slow-moving, closed mid/upper low pressure over the Canada
Maritimes is helping to send wrap- around moisture in northeast
flow across much of New England, within a broad cyclonic mid- 
level flow. This is leading to mostly cloudy skies this 
afternoon with scattered hit-or- mostly-miss light showers, with
northeast winds around 10 mph. Expect these conditions to 
generally hold steady through the afternoon, with the best shot 
at light showers being in interior Southern New England. However
later tonight and overnight, a compact but pretty robust 
shortwave evident in afternoon water vapor imagery well north of
Montreal digs south- southeastward through New England, 
supporting at least a continuation of mostly cloudy conditions, 
but also support a risk for showers spreading back eastward 
overnight into early Sunday. By mid to late Sunday morning, 
subsidence in the wake of this disturbance brings decreased 
cloud cover with more sunshine and lighter northerly winds into 
Sunday afternoon. Any showers this afternoon into early Sunday 
won't amount to much in terms of impacts, but there will be some
showers to dodge at times. 

Northerly to northeast flow this weekend combined with rising 
astronomical tides support a risk for very minor coastal 
flooding around the evening high tides tonight and again on 
Sunday night for the Cape and Islands. A coastal flood advisory 
has been issued for tonight's high tide, and another advisory or
coastal flood statement could be needed again for Sunday 
night's high tide. Overall minor impacts anticipated to the 
typically more vulnerable spots (Easy Street on Nantucket and 
Sesuit Harbor in Dennis). There is also an high risk for rip 
currents along east-facing shorelines in eastern MA, as offshore
seas rise to around 4-6 ft overnight into Sunday.

Cloudy conditions and northeast breezes will help offset modest
cool advection tonight, leading to lows in the mid to upper 
50s. Highs Sunday top out in the upper 60s near the eastern 
coastline with the onshore flow, but should reach into the low 
to mid 70s under increasing sunshine by afternoon elsewhere.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry conditions Labor Day through much of 
Wednesday. Pattern becomes more unsettled Wednesday night into 
late-week with periods of showers possible and gusty winds
possible Thursday. 

The deeper mid-level trough shifts further eastward through the
day Monday while higher heights advect in as a mid-level ridge 
builds to the west. This will bring in warmer temperatures aloft
with 925mb temperatures +15-17C. NW flow and a sufficiently 
mixed boundary layer accompanied mainly clear skies should help 
yield high temperatures in the the mid to upper 70s for most. 
High pressure will support mainly dry conditions Monday with 
similar conditions and temperatures likely for Tuesday under the
same pattern. 

Ensemble guidance shows a signal for a transition to a more 
unsettled pattern mid to late week. Flow aloft becomes more 
zonal with a few embedded shortwave troughs moving through late 
Wednesday through late-week. This should be accompanied by a 
plume of above normal moisture (120-150% of normal) and a jet 
positioned to supply lift across the region. This should be 
enough to support periods of showers later Wednesday/Wednesday 
night into Friday. There is spread across guidance in the finer 
details of the timing of the waves which will influence timing 
of the showers. Overall, there isn't a strong signal for flash 
flooding at this time. Marginal instability in place may owe to 
a storm or downpour depending on the timing. 

Another thing we will need to monitor is the potential for a 
period of gusty winds Thursday. An 850mb 35-45kt LLJ positions 
across southern New England into Thursday. If winds mix down 
efficiently, this would support gusty winds. There is a signal 
for anomalously gusty winds on the ECMWF EFI (still fairly far 
out). Flow looks to become more westerly behind the passage of 
the first wave with a signal for CAA. Both things that could 
facilitate the mixing down of the higher winds aloft (to some 
extent at least). As mentioned, timing of these waves are lower 
confidence and this could have influence on when we get the 
better mixing and thus the gusty winds. So plenty of details to 
be worked out. If things align, ensembles show potential for 
gusts in the 30-40 mph range on Thursday across the land and 
coastal waters. Still plenty of details to work out in the 
pattern before we come into better agreement about the gusts, 
but something to watch for now.
